findings.quote: the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 5: numeral style breaks with the rest of the piece, which spells out every comparable quantity ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'about forty minutes'); a copy editor would regularise. Rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places'.

findings.quote: a lift, a scrape, a fresh lamp and a relay take about forty minutes
findings.note: class 3: 'a relay' used as a noun for re-laying the buoy collides with the ordinary sense of 'relay'; the trade spelling is hyphenated. Rewrite: 'a lift, a scrape, a fresh lamp and a re-lay take about forty minutes'.

findings.quote: the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees
findings.note: class 3: 'stand' in the temperature sense governs 'at' ('the mercury stood at thirty'); with 'the space' as subject the preposition is dropped and the verb reads bare. Rewrite: 'the space near the ridge can stand at close to thirty degrees'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3: bat boxes are put up or fitted, not 'opened', and the next sentence uses the right verb ('those fitted between September and February'), so the inconsistency is visible within the paragraph. Rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'.

findings.quote: through the spring floods, the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 3: 'spring floods' is not the phrase a British marine writer uses for what swings a moored buoy. An editor reads it either as river snowmelt (the Swedish 'varflod') or as a mangled 'spring tides'; the excursion driver at a sea buoy is the spring tidal stream, and the passage elsewhere keeps trade terms exact ('scope', 'sinker', 'swivel'). Editor's rewrite: 'through the spring tides, the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together'.

class 4: numeral style breaks the passage's own convention - every other measure is spelled out ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'about forty minutes'). Editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3: collocation miss - a bat box is fitted, hung or put up, not 'opened' (buildings and exhibitions open; boxes do not). The passage itself uses the right verbs everywhere else ('those fitted between September and February', 'twenty-four boxes went up on nine buildings', 'You can hang the finest box in the county'), so the outlier reads as a slip rather than a choice. Editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'.

findings.quote: the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees
findings.note: class 3: 'stand' before a figure normally takes 'at' ('the temperature stood at thirty degrees'), and with 'the space' as subject against the parallel clause's 'sits ten or twelve degrees below it' the bare 'stand close to' reads clipped. Editor's rewrite: 'the space near the ridge can sit at close to thirty degrees'.
